title: Investing Fascia–Carotid Sheath Mechanical Coupling Framework: A Mechanistic Narrative Review of Intravascular, Lymphatic, and Autonomic Neural Effects Within the Sheath
content: Background and objective: The carotid sheath is a mechanical hub between superficial mechanical loads in the neck and deep neurovascular function. This article organizes the evidence at each node within the “investing fascia–carotid sheath mechanical coupling” framework, evaluates its evidence maturity and key gaps, and provides a testable node checklist for subsequent synchronized measurement studies.Methods: This article is a mechanistic narrative review. Literature inclusion used purposive sampling. PubMed, Web of Science, and Scopus were searched through October 31, 2026. No language restriction was applied, and the included literature was predominantly English, including one Chinese-language article. Inclusion criteria were provision of primary human evidence for the node, key animal functional evidence, methodological anchors, or key integrative reviews. Peer-reviewed original studies published online ahead of print were eligible, whereas preprints, conference abstracts, and unpublished registered trials were excluded. Standardized search and dual-reviewer screening procedures for systematic reviews were not used. Evidence maturity ratings were single-author integrative assessments based on study design and evidence type, without independent dual rating, and are not equivalent to risk-of-bias assessment in systematic reviews. An updated search will be performed before submission for literature published between October 31, 2026, and the submission date. If newly identified literature changes any node rating, this will be stated at revision.Key findings: Each node was supported by separate evidence, but causal connections between nodes have not been tested within the same study. The mechanical starting point involves both mechanical and biochemical molecular pathways, a cross-organ Piezo–ECM positive-feedback background, in vivo shear wave elastography (SWE) reliability, and direct measurements of pressure to the deep cervical fascia. However, the in vivo mechanical state of the investing fascia has not been linked to intrasheath variables. The arterial end has evidence of PIEZO functional necessity, human expression, ex vivo decomposition of wall–receptor responses, human electrical stimulation/mechanical compression intervention data, and a human quantitative precedent for transmission efficiency from external pressure to the carotid sinus; however, “fascial mechanical exposure–change in receptor function” has not been directly observed. The venous end has evidence of acute external compression sensitivity, improved flow after structural decompression, and observational associations in clinical populations; however, chronic fascial tension has not been covered, and the clinical associations are non-causal. The lymphatic node has human histological evidence, histopathological evidence, in vivo content load, animal functional resistance, dynamic contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging (DCE-MRI)/T1 mapping methodology, and drainage surrogate endpoints; neck lymph node dissection cohorts and animal mechanisms suggest that lymphatic structural injury can impair brain lymphatic clearance and synaptic protein homeostasis, but the exposure is not investing fascia mechanics. The sympathetic node has anatomical quantification, mechanical compression–induced changes in muscle sympathetic nerve activity (MSNA), dose–response, and sham-controlled randomized controlled trial (RCT) evidence. However, the sign of the net effect of “sympathetic trunk compression–induced activation vs. baroreceptor compression–induced inhibition” remains uncertain. This node is rated moderate-to-high (molecular functional necessity limitedly satisfied); subtype definitions and thresholds are provided in Section 2 of the main text. The vagus node has anatomical variation, side-specific cross-sectional area (CSA) baseline, single-fiber recording methodology, and a same-individual structure–function pairing precedent; however, single-fiber activity has not been recorded under mechanical intervention. At the mechanotransduction level, there is evidence of PIEZO expression; however, functional activation under chronic mechanical exposure has not been tested in humans. In adjacent fields, a methodological precedent exists for same-individual joint analysis of “local tissue SWE + baroreflex function,” but the target was not the investing fascia. The seven node ratings are as follows: mechanical starting point, moderate; arterial end, moderate-to-high; venous end, moderate; lymphatic node, moderate; sympathetic node, moderate-to-high (molecular functional necessity limitedly satisfied); vagus node, moderate; and mechanotransduction, moderate-to-low. The direct intervention evidence status for the fascia–sheath interface in Section 3.8 is “preliminary”; it does not constitute an independent maturity level and does not participate in the seven-node rating.Conclusions: The evidence at each node separately supports different components of the framework, but causal connections between nodes have not yet been tested within the same study. Structural change and functional impairment may dissociate, the sign of the net sympathetic effect is uncertain, and the mechanistic rationale for deep cervical lymphatic–venous anastomosis (dcLVA) is questionable, constituting three competing explanations. The core gap is that “investing fascia mechanical state–intrasheath mechanical environment–target-structure functional marker” have never been synchronously measured in the same participant within the same time frame; this gap requires an answer from one or a group of multicenter studies using the same synchronized measurement paradigm. Several methodological anchors in the existing literature (e.g., the quantitative recording paradigm for transmission of external pressure to the carotid sinus, the directional difference between acute mechanical stimulation and chronic mechanical constraint, and the human feasibility of fascia–sheath interface intervention) can be reintegrated to support a synchronized measurement design, but they do not change the core gap judgment.
